parts.title: Course enquiry
parts.context_zh: 第一部分：一位男士打电话给社区中心，咨询陶艺课

lines.en: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre, Sarah speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about the evening classes. I saw something about a beginners' course in pottery.
Yes, the pottery course. It starts next month, and there are still a few places left. Shall I take your details?
Yes, please.
Can I have your name?
It's David Hartley. That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.
lines.say: It's David Hartley. That's H. A. R. T. L. E. Y.

lines.en: Thank you, Mr Hartley. And a contact number?
My mobile's best. It's 07946 381 552.
lines.say: My mobile's best. It's oh seven nine four six, three eight one, five five two.

lines.en: Lovely. And can I ask how you heard about the course? Was it from our website?
No, I haven't looked at the website, actually. A friend mentioned it a while ago, but what made me call was an advert in the local newspaper.
Great, I'll put that down. Now, the classes run on Tuesday evenings.
Oh, really? I thought it said Thursday.
It used to be on Thursdays, but we've moved it to Tuesdays this term. Is that all right for you?
Yes, Tuesday's fine. What time does it start?
The building opens at a quarter to seven, but the class itself starts at 7.15, and it finishes at nine.
lines.say: The building opens at a quarter to seven, but the class itself starts at seven fifteen, and it finishes at nine.

lines.en: OK. And how much does the course cost?
The full price is 120 pounds for ten weeks, but there's a reduced price of 95 pounds for people who live in the area. Do you live locally?
lines.say: The full price is one hundred and twenty pounds for ten weeks, but there's a reduced price of ninety-five pounds for people who live in the area. Do you live locally?

lines.en: Yes, I'm on Mill Road, just round the corner.
Then it's the lower price for you. That includes all the clay and the cost of firing your pots in the kiln.
Do I need to bring anything? Tools, or special clothes?
The tools are provided, but it can get quite messy, so please bring an apron.
Right. And where exactly are the classes held? I've only been in the main hall before.
They're not in the main hall. They're in the Garden Room, which is at the back of the building.
And is there somewhere to park?
Our own car park is closed in the evenings, I'm afraid, but you can use the free car park behind the library. It's only two minutes' walk.
That's fine. And how do I pay? Can I pay by card when I come in?
You can pay by card online. But if you'd rather pay at reception, we only take cash, I'm afraid.
I'll come in and pay with cash, then. Thanks very much for your help.

parts.title: Volunteer induction
parts.context_zh: 第二部分：湿地保护中心的志愿者协调员给新志愿者做入职介绍

lines.en: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartfield Wetland Centre. My name's Peter, and I'm the volunteer coordinator. Before you start your first shift, I'd like to give you a bit of background and go through a few practical things.

The centre opened in 1998 on the site of an old gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and over the years they've become home to a huge variety of birds, insects and plants. People often assume the land was always a nature reserve, or that it used to be farmland, but in fact it was industrial land for nearly fifty years.
lines.say: The centre opened in nineteen ninety-eight on the site of an old gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and over the years they've become home to a huge variety of birds, insects and plants. People often assume the land was always a nature reserve, or that it used to be farmland, but in fact it was industrial land for nearly fifty years.

lines.en: We get around forty thousand visitors a year. Most people come at weekends, of course, and summer is busy, but our busiest time is actually the spring school holidays, when the young birds hatch.

Now, what will you be doing? Many of you told me you'd like to work outdoors, on the reserve itself. That will come, but for the first month all new volunteers work in the visitor centre, helping at the information desk. That way you get to know the site and the people who visit it.

On the subject of guided walks: we used to run them every day, but we found that many visitors preferred to explore on their own, so now we only run them on Sunday mornings. They're very popular, so booking is essential.

One thing I must stress is safety. The paths are generally easy, but the boardwalks over the water can be slippery after rain. And the most important rule of all: please make sure visitors never feed the birds bread. It's bad for them, and it pollutes the water. If people ask, we sell proper bird food in the shop.

Right, let me tell you about some of the areas of the reserve. The first place most visitors head for is the Reed Bed Hide. A hide, if you don't know, is a small building where you can watch wildlife without being seen. This one is especially good for spotting otters. We've seen them there at least once a week this year.
Next is the Meadow. In early summer it's full of wild flowers, and it's the best place on the site to see butterflies.

Then there's the Children's Discovery Zone. This includes a pond-dipping area, where children use nets to look at the creatures living in the water. Sessions start every half hour and last about 20 minutes.
lines.say: Then there's the Children's Discovery Zone. This includes a pond-dipping area, where children use nets to look at the creatures living in the water. Sessions start every half hour and last about twenty minutes.

lines.en: Over on the east side is the Lookout Tower. It's 12 metres high, and from the top you can see right across the reserve. Unfortunately there's no lift, so it isn't suitable for wheelchair users.
lines.say: Over on the east side is the Lookout Tower. It's twelve metres high, and from the top you can see right across the reserve. Unfortunately there's no lift, so it isn't suitable for wheelchair users.

lines.en: And finally, the café. It's just been completely renovated, and it now has a terrace overlooking the main lake, which I'm sure will be very popular once the weather warms up.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.why: 建在废弃的砾石采石场上；农田和自然保护区都是他说“人们常以为”的错误印象。

items.at: for the first month all new volunteers work in the visitor centre, helping at the information desk
items.why: 户外工作以后才会有，第一个月都在游客中心的问讯台。

items.at: now we only run them on Sunday mornings
items.why: 以前每天都有（used to），现在只在周日上午。

items.q: What is the most important rule for visitors?
options: Do not give bread to the birds.
Stay off the boardwalks after rain.
Buy bird food only in the shop.
items.at: please make sure visitors never feed the birds bread
items.why: the most important rule of all：不许喂面包。木栈道只是说雨后滑，没说不能走。

items.at: especially good for spotting otters

parts.title: A research project on urban beekeeping
parts.context_zh: 第三部分：两个学生（Maya 和 Ben）和导师讨论城市养蜂的调查项目

lines.en: Come in, Maya, Ben. So, how's the beekeeping project going?
Pretty well, I think. We've finished the survey and most of the interviews.
Good. Remind me why you chose this topic. Was it because of your uncle, Ben? You mentioned he keeps bees.
He does, but that wasn't really the reason. I'd never been that interested, to be honest.
What actually got us started was a news report saying that the number of beehives in London had more than doubled in ten years. We wondered who all these new beekeepers were.
Fair enough. And how did the questionnaire go?

We got more responses than we expected, about eighty. The problem was that quite a few people misunderstood one of the questions. We asked how many hives they had, and some people counted the boxes inside each hive instead.

That happens. Make sure you explain how you dealt with it in the methodology section. Now, I've read your draft. The literature review is a reasonable length, but most of your sources are more than ten years old. You really need to include more recent studies.
OK, we'll look for some.
What did you find about the beekeepers themselves?
That was the surprising part. We expected most of them to be people who'd kept bees for decades, but in fact the majority had started in the last five years.
And fewer than half of them belonged to a beekeeping club, which was also unexpected.
Interesting. So what are your next steps?
I'm going to redo the charts. They're a bit hard to read at the moment.
And I'll contact the local council. We want to find out whether there are any rules about keeping bees in gardens.
Good. Now, let's talk about the presentation next week. You've got five sections. What are you planning to do with the introduction?
We think it's too long at the moment, so we'll make it shorter. We'll keep the main points, though.
And the section on the history of beekeeping?
Honestly, it isn't really relevant to our research question, so we've decided to drop it completely.
I agree. What about the survey results?
At the moment it's just numbers. We're going to add some photos of the hives we visited, so people can picture what we're talking about.
Good idea. And the interviews?
We were going to cut some of the quotations, but we've decided they work well as they are. We won't change that section.
And finally, the problems you faced?
We've got that near the beginning, but it would make more sense to discuss it after the results. So we'll move it to the end.
That sounds like a sensible plan.

parts.title: The development of the bicycle
parts.context_zh: 第四部分：一场关于自行车发展史的讲座

lines.en: Today I'm going to talk about the bicycle, a machine that most of us take for granted, but which had a surprisingly large effect on society.

The story usually begins in 1817, with a German inventor called Karl von Drais. His machine had two wheels and could be steered, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet, rather like a child's balance bike today.
lines.say: The story usually begins in eighteen seventeen, with a German inventor called Karl von Drais. His machine had two wheels and could be steered, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet, rather like a child's balance bike today.

lines.en: In the 1860s, pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, creating what was called the velocipede. In Britain, people gave it a less flattering name: the boneshaker. With iron tyres on rough or cobbled roads, you can imagine why.
lines.say: In the eighteen sixties, pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, creating what was called the velocipede. In Britain, people gave it a less flattering name: the boneshaker. With iron tyres on rough or cobbled roads, you can imagine why.

lines.en: Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the bigger that wheel was, the further the bicycle travelled with each turn. So in the 1870s, designers made the front wheel larger and larger, producing the high-wheeler, which gave riders much greater speed. The problem was that the rider sat so high that any obstacle could send them flying over the handlebars, and serious falls were common.
lines.say: Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the bigger that wheel was, the further the bicycle travelled with each turn. So in the eighteen seventies, designers made the front wheel larger and larger, producing the high-wheeler, which gave riders much greater speed. The problem was that the rider sat so high that any obstacle could send them flying over the handlebars, and serious falls were common.

lines.en: The solution came in 1885 with the Rover, often called the first safety bicycle. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the pedals drove the back wheel by means of a chain. Riders could now go fast without sitting dangerously high.
lines.say: The solution came in eighteen eighty-five with the Rover, often called the first safety bicycle. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the pedals drove the back wheel by means of a chain. Riders could now go fast without sitting dangerously high.

lines.en: Three years later, in 1888, John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled tyre. Interestingly, he wasn't thinking about bicycles at all: he wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. But the air-filled tyre made cycling far smoother, and within a few years it was standard.
lines.say: Three years later, in eighteen eighty-eight, John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled tyre. Interestingly, he wasn't thinking about bicycles at all: he wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. But the air-filled tyre made cycling far smoother, and within a few years it was standard.

lines.en: So what were the social effects? First, the bicycle gave ordinary people a cheap way to travel. A bicycle cost far less than keeping a horse, which needed feeding and stabling every day.
This had an impact on where people lived. Workers no longer had to live within walking distance of their workplace, so towns began to spread outwards.
The bicycle was also important for women. It gave them a new kind of independence, and it led to changes in clothing, as long, heavy skirts were simply impractical on a bicycle.

Cyclists also became an organised group with political influence. In both Britain and the United States, they campaigned for better road surfaces, years before cars became common. In a sense, the smooth roads that motorists later enjoyed were first demanded by cyclists.
And today, of course, many cities are encouraging cycling again. Pollution is often mentioned, but the main reason given by most city governments is to reduce congestion.
